description: We are a multidisciplinary team from Kazakhstan with skills in robotics, aerospace, software, data analysis, astrophysics and Earth science. We aim to turn NASA data into useful tools.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a web tool for exploring images from NASA's SPHEREx mission and watching how objects in the sky change over time. SPHEREx surveys the whole sky in 102 infrared bands (0.75–5 µm) and revisits each region many times, but the raw archive is noisy, full of artifacts, and hard for non-specialists to use.

Our tool connects directly to NASA's IRSA archive. A user enters a target or coordinates and chooses a wavelength, detector, and field of view. SPHEREx Blink then cuts out the region, cleans the background, reprojects the frames onto a common grid, and shows them in an interactive Aladin sky viewer. It also builds a light curve for the target. Every point is checked for quality, and when a point is rejected, the tool shows why, including the contamination flags behind the decision. Views can be shared through a URL.

We deliberately used a transparent algorithm instead of a black-box AI, with a human making the final call. This keeps results verifiable and explainable. SPHEREx Blink makes fresh data from a new mission usable by students, citizen scientists, and researchers, and lowers the barrier to discovery.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works

SPHEREx Blink is a web tool and Python library that turns raw SPHEREx observations into images and measurements people can actually explore. You can enter the name of an object (the tool resolves it through SIMBAD) or type in RA and Dec coordinates. You then choose a wavelength, a detector and a field of view.

The backend requests FITS cutouts directly from the NASA IRSA archive. It removes cosmic rays and hot pixels by checking each pixel against its eight neighbors. This happens before any interpolation, so a single bad pixel cannot spread and turn into a fake object. Next it masks pixels marked with contamination flags (ghosts, crosstalk, streaks, bloom, halos and saturation). Then it subtracts the background, first the zodiacal light model and then a sigma clipped median. After that every frame is reprojected onto one common sky grid. Observations are grouped into epochs, and any epoch longer than 20 days is split so that fast moving objects do not smear.

The frames are shown in an interactive Aladin Lite sky viewer and can be exported as a blink animation (GIF), so motion and changes in brightness are easy to see. The tool also builds a light curve and a spectrum. Every point is labeled as validated, provisional or rejected, and the tool shows the reason for each rejection.

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx data is new, very large and hard for non specialists to use. Our tool cuts the path from a question to a visual answer down to a single web request, and it does this without hiding how reliable the data is. It is built for students, educators, citizen scientists and researchers who want to check a target quickly. Our goal is to help more people explore a new NASA mission and notice objects that deserve a closer look.

Tools and technologies

The backend is written in Python with FastAPI, astropy, astroquery and reproject. The data comes from the NASA IRSA archive (SPHEREx cutouts), and object names are resolved through SIMBAD. The frontend is a single page application in HTML and JavaScript with Aladin Lite 3.8.2 (CDS Strasbourg). Results are cached in PostgreSQL through Supabase, which also makes it possible to share results by URL. The project is deployed on Vercel and covered by a pytest suite with 343 passing tests.

How it is creative

Instead of a black box AI, every step of our pipeline is transparent, and the final decision is made by a human, much like in the Backyard Worlds citizen science project. The tool does more than display data. It explains why each point was kept or rejected. Blink animations make changes over time visible at a glance.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty. The tool keeps what is visible in the frames separate from what is a confirmed measurement. When we tested the five challenge targets, we reported our limitations openly. Only a small share of photometry points passed strict validation, and we do not claim confirmed proper motion.

Data quality. SPHEREx pixels are large (about 6 arcseconds) and the images contain many artifacts, so we built filtering at several stages.

Security. Downloads are allowed only from IRSA hosts, and frontend libraries are pinned to exact versions.

Accessibility and reproducibility. The tool runs in any browser, results can be shared by URL, and the Python library lets researchers run the same pipeline on their own computers.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Data at NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA)
